prompt: Design the account page for Fernhill Library's online card sign-up. Fields: full name, email, password, date of birth, and an optional checkbox for event emails. Show the page in the state right after the person pressed the button with two problems: the email they typed has no @ and the password is 6 characters (the rule is at least 12). The person's other entries are already filled in. Return one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, no external assets, fonts, scripts or images.
rubric: Every field has a visible label above or outside the input, not only placeholder text.
A summary near the top lists both problems, and each problem is reachable from it (links or equivalent).
Each error appears at its field and says in plain words how to fix it, rather than just 'invalid'.
The values the person typed (name, date of birth, the bad email) are still shown in the fields.
Errors are signaled by more than color, such as an icon or text prefix.
The button names the action (for example 'Create account') and sits directly under the last field.

prompt: Our checkout spec says: floating labels on every field, the Pay button stays disabled until every field is valid, fields turn red as you type, every field has an asterisk, and phone number is required. List the changes you would make, most important first, with one line of reasoning each.
rubric: Flags the disabled Pay button and recommends keeping it pressable with errors explained after the press.
Flags errors that appear while typing and proposes checking on submit, then re-checking fields already in error.
Replaces floating labels with static visible labels above the fields.
Questions the required phone number, asking for a stated reason or making it optional.
Replaces blanket asterisks by marking the minority (usually optional fields) in words.
The list is ordered by impact and each item carries a short reason.

prompt: We want to ask 'How did you hear about us?' with four answers on a sign-up form. Dropdown, radio group, or free text? Answer in under 120 words.
rubric: Recommends visible radio buttons for the four answers (or argues convincingly for dropping the question).
Notes the question should be optional or deferred until after sign-up.
Mentions an 'Other' choice with a text field if answers might not fit.
Stays under 120 words.

prompt: Outline the structure (no code) for an online insurance claim that has about 40 questions, several that depend on earlier answers, needs photos and a police report, and usually takes people two or three days to finish.
rubric: Opens with a page before the first question that lists what the person needs (documents, photos, time, eligibility).
Uses a task list with a status for each section.
Supports saving and resuming across days.
Handles the branching sections with one topic per page rather than one huge page.
Asks for photos and the police report inside the task that needs them.
Ends with a review of answers and a confirmation that says what happens next.

prompt:
Improve this login form markup and explain each change briefly. Show the corrected markup. ```html

Welcome back

Enter the code we texted you

```
rubric: Adds real, associated visible labels (for/id or wrapping) instead of relying on placeholders.
Email field uses an email input type with an email autofill token and turns off auto-capitalize and auto-correct.
Password field gets the current-password autofill token.
Replaces the six code boxes with one field using the one-time-code autofill token and a numeric keypad.
Renames 'Submit' to a specific verb such as 'Sign in'.
Removes the auto-advance script.

prompt: A product manager asks why we shouldn't show email errors while the user is typing. Answer in under 150 words.
rubric: Explains that a half-typed value is not yet wrong, so the early message is false or noisy.
Mentions a cost of premature or blur-time errors, such as autofill, switching windows, or annoyance.
Recommends checking on submit and re-checking fields that already show an error.
Stays under 150 words and is not dogmatic (acknowledges exceptions such as password checklists).

prompt: Design step 3 of 4 of a grocery checkout: choosing a delivery slot. Offer six slots across two days, each with a time window and a fee, plus a short order summary. Return one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, no external assets, fonts, scripts or images.
rubric: The step and count appear in the heading text (for example 'Delivery slot, step 3 of 4').
The slots are a single-choice control showing the time window and the fee together so they can be compared.
There is one primary button that names the next step, placed under the content and aligned with it.
A way back that keeps earlier answers is present.
The page shows the order summary and does not carry full site navigation that competes with the task.

prompt: Design a pricing section comparing three subscription plans for a note-taking app, with a recommended plan. Return one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, no external assets, fonts, scripts or images.
rubric: The three plans are easy to compare side by side.
Prices are the most prominent element in each plan.
Feature rows line up across the plans.
The recommended plan is marked with a text label, not by color alone.
No form fields, validation messages or step indicators appear that the brief did not ask for.

prompt: Design a macOS-style preferences sheet for a desktop photo app: export format, quality slider, color profile, and Cancel / Save buttons, following macOS conventions. Return one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, no external assets, fonts, scripts or images.
rubric: Labels sit to the left of their controls, in the platform's two-column arrangement.
Cancel and Save sit at the bottom right with the default action (Save) rightmost.
The primary action is visually distinct from Cancel.
Does not import web form patterns such as top-aligned labels, a left-aligned submit button or an error summary.
Export format, quality, and color profile each use a fitting control.

prompt: Add a newsletter sign-up to the footer of a website for a small bakery: one email field and a button. Return one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, no external assets, fonts, scripts or images.
rubric: The sign-up stays a compact single row (field and button) inside the footer.
The field has an accessible name, either a visible label or a visually hidden one, and any placeholder reads as an example address.
The button text says what happens (for example 'Subscribe').
The email field uses an email input type.
No error summary panel, step indicator or extra fields are added.
